scenes.desc: Huelva reclama la cuna del fandango andaluz y es la provincia con más estilos: las antologías recogen más de treinta y cinco, locales (Encinasola, el Alosno, Cabezas Rubias, Calañas, el Andévalo, Valverde del Camino) y personales, creados por profesionales como Paco Isidro, Pepe Rebollo, el Comía, Antonio Rengel, Pérez de Guzmán y Paco Toronjo; de fuera dejaron su sello el Gloria, Macandé, el Carbonerillo y Manolo Caracol. Paco Toronjo, fijo en los festivales desde finales de los sesenta y en las bienales de Sevilla, les dio una jondura difícil de imitar. El baile, de pareja y galanteo, se ve ya poco.

scenes.name: Los cantes de Levante o de las minas
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Nacidos del trabajo en las minas del siglo XIX en las sierras de Cartagena y La Unión y en Linares, La Carolina y Andújar: cantes de dolor profundo sobre la mina, sus accidentes y los compañeros muertos, hechos con fandangos regionales, murcianas, malagueñas y el cante de madrugá de los mineros. La taranta, el más significativo, tiene dos estilos, el de Linares (Gabriel Moreno, Carmen Linares) y el de La Unión (Encarnación Fernández, Pepe Cros), y Camarón le puso dulzura; el taranto, almeriense, tiene compás porque nació para el baile de Carmen Amaya en los cuarenta, con el Ciego de la Playa y Pedro el Morato. La cartagenera, de temas más urbanos, la fijó Antonio Chacón a finales del XIX y la cantaron Cayetano Muriel, Manuel Centeno, Manuel Torre y la Niña de los Peines. La minera se atribuye a Rojo el Alpargatero, Antonio Grau Mora, que hacia 1885 abrió en La Unión una posada que acabó en café cantante y oía cantar a los mineros de madrugada: es el gran creador de los cantes mineros. Las granaínas, de Frasquito Yerbabuena y sobre todo Chacón, son un cante casi barroco hoy cargado de vibratos operísticos. Sin minas, los concursos de Linares y La Unión mantienen vivos estos cantes.

scenes.name: Las cantiñas: alegrías, caracoles, mirabrás y romeras
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Cantes alegres de la bahía de Cádiz, en compás de soleá y muy ligados al baile, que arranca majestuoso y va ganando fuerza hasta desplantes electrizantes. Nacen probablemente de la jotilla gaditana, hermanada con la jota aragonesa por la resistencia común contra Napoleón, de ahí las letras sobre la guerra y el mar; la leyenda atribuye su creación a Enrique el Mellizo, que oyó a una muchacha cantar jotas con un ciego. Tomaron identidad en la segunda mitad del XIX. Hay cantiñas del Pinini de Utrera y Lebrija y de Córdoba; la rosa ya no se canta. Las alegrías, al principio baile de mujer sola, se hicieron más lentas a comienzos del XX y empiezan con el «tirititrán» que, según Chano Lobato, inventó Pericón de Cádiz al olvidar la letra; las cantaron el Mellizo, Ignacio Ezpeleta, Aurelio Sellés, Manolo Vargas y Pericón. Los caracoles, de Tío José el Granaíno (picador del Chiclanero), los recreó Chacón y triunfaron en Madrid («la gran calle de Alcalá»). El mirabrás son alegrías largas (José Menese, con letras de Moreno Galván), y las romeras se atribuyen al Granaíno o a una cantaora llamada la Romera. Hoy el gran intérprete es Chano Lobato.

scenes.name: Los tangos, tientos y marianas
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Con bulerías y cantiñas, el gran cante festero: letras de vida, amor y muerte con cierta ligereza, ritmo vivo y pegadizo fácil de seguir con palmas, y un baile sensual. Cádiz y Sevilla se disputan su paternidad, pero los hay en toda Andalucía y en Extremadura; Triana tiene el estilo del Titi y Jerez su propio sello. Su origen musical se discute: Mairena los tenía por cante básico gitano; los estudios recientes los llevan a Cuba y las habaneras llegadas a Sevilla y Cádiz en la segunda mitad del XIX; los granadinos defienden una raíz morisca (el disco Granada canta por tangos recoge trece estilos, entre ellos los de la morería). Manuel Ríos Ruiz concluye que no se sabe con certeza. La Niña de los Peines se hizo inmortal con su copla «Péinate tú con mis peines». Del tango nacen los tientos, más pausados y solemnes, que cantaron primero el Mellizo y el Marrurro y se popularizaron a comienzos del XX, y la mariana, que difundió Bernardo el de los Lobitos y hoy casi solo canta Pepe Menese con letras de Moreno Galván.

scenes.name: Las soleares
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: La madre del cante y uno de sus pilares, independiente de cualquier otro ritmo; los cantaores la consideran «el toro bravo del arte jondo». Coplas solemnes y sentenciosas de tres o cuatro octosílabos, unidas por la guitarra, que suelen rematarse por bulerías; muy apropiadas para el baile de mujer. Se desarrolló al sur del Guadalquivir desde los jaleos festivos: la primera mención es de la Andonda en Triana hacia 1840, una cantaora temible contemporánea del Fillo, y tomó su forma actual entre 1875 y 1915. Las mujeres fueron clave en su creación y transmisión (la Andonda, Mercedes la Serneta, Fernanda de Utrera, Carmen Linares). Hay soleares de Triana (la Andonda, Silverio, Fernando el de Triana, la Niña de los Peines, Tomás Pavón, Mairena), de Alcalá, más solemnes (Joaquín el de la Paula, Juan Talega), de Utrera (la Serneta, el Pinini, María Peña, Fernanda), de Cádiz y el Puerto, más jondas (Enrique Butrón, el Mellizo, Paquirri el Guanté), de Jerez, breves y llenas de melismas (Curro Frijones, José Illanda, Juan Mojama, Tío José de Paula, Manuel Torre) y de Córdoba, más pausadas.

scenes.name: Las siguiriyas, livianas y serranas
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Una de las expresiones más dramáticas y de los palos más importantes: sin siguiriyas y soleares el flamenco no sería lo que es. Un quejío entero de lamentos que no admite medias tintas («con las siguiriyas no se puede vender la burra»), con coplas trágicas de cuatro versos (6, 6, 10 y 6 sílabas), muchas sobre la muerte de los seres queridos, y falsetas lentas que suenan a campanas a muerto. Lorca la describió como un grito terrible que divide el paisaje en dos; Tía Anica la Piriñaca decía que cuando la cantaba a gusto la boca le sabía a sangre. La cantaban ya el Planeta (la de la Luna, la más antigua conocida) y el Fillo; luego Manuel Torre, Silverio, Paco la Luz, Cagancho, el Nitri, Curro Dulce, el Loco Mateo, el Mellizo, Terremoto de Jerez (que cantó toda la noche por siguiriyas con su madre muerta en brazos) y Juan Talega; hoy el Chocolate y José Menese. Antonio Mairena grabó unas cuarenta y cinco formas: es el siguiriyero más importante. Sus escuelas son Jerez y los Puertos, Cádiz y Triana. En el baile la difundió Vicente Escudero y Pilar López le añadió los palillos. La liviana, cante de campo, caminos y bandoleros, prepara la voz para la serrana, a la que Silverio dio brillo y con la que se remata por siguiriyas.

scenes.name: La caña, el polo y la petenera
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Tres cantes de la familia de la soleá. La caña, con ayes más arrastrados, se sitúa en la serranía de Ronda (un viajero inglés la oyó allí en 1830) o en la voz árabe gaunia, «canción»; la cantaron el Fillo, Tío José el Granaíno, Antonio Chacón, Pepe de la Matrona y Rafael Romero el Gallina, y hoy se usa más para el baile solemne. El polo se cantaba tras la caña, con la misma métrica; el de Tobalo, su supuesto creador, aparece ya en Estébanez Calderón y hoy se usa en la soleá apolá; Enrique Morente grabó el de Chacón. La petenera, melancólica y de origen incierto, se atribuye a una mujer de Paterna de la Ribera, «la perdición de los hombres», o a los sefardíes de los Balcanes; los gitanos la evitaron porque traía mala suerte. La cantaron la Niña de los Peines, Naranjito de Triana, Rafael Romero, Fosforito y hoy Pepe Menese.

scenes.name: Los cantes de Málaga: malagueñas, rondeñas, jaberas y verdiales
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Después de Sevilla y Cádiz, Málaga es la provincia con más variedad de cantes. La malagueña, cante libre, sin medida y sin baile, de rico toque, ha influido en las granaínas y en todos los cantes minero-levantinos. Nació en Álora (las malagueñas perotas) a partir de los fandangos abandolaos, acompañados de bandola; tras los anónimos y los de Cipriano Pitana, Francisco Jiménez y Joaquín Tabaco, Juan Breva le dio identidad propia, y Lorca escribió de su trino. Su esplendor es la segunda mitad del XIX, con el Canario, la Trini, Baldomero Pacheco y Fosforito el Viejo; también firmaron malagueñas el Mellizo, único gitano creador de una (inspirada en el prefacio de la misa), y Chacón. Diego Clavel recogió treinta y una en los noventa. La rondeña, de principios del XIX y de la tierra del Tobalo, es la pieza con que muchos guitarristas abren sus conciertos; la jabera, ruda y difícil, debe su nombre a una vendedora de habas y está casi perdida; los verdiales, de probable raíz morisca, apenas han cambiado y conservan la panda con violín, panderos, chinchines y cañas para la fiesta de san Juan.

scenes.name: Los tanguillos de Cádiz
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Vinculados al carnaval de Cádiz, son el soporte de chirigotas, coros y murgas; cantados en grupo pierden su naturaleza flamenca, que es individual, aunque como baile la conservan. Hay constancia de los «tangos graciosos» del barrio de La Viña en 1779, en la tonadilla La anónima de Tomás Abril, y el tango americano o de negros terminó de formarlos. Letras jocosas y satíricas: «el chiste ingenuo y feliz enfrente de la tragedia jonda del quejío» (Emilio Jiménez Díaz). Aurelio y Pericón de Cádiz, Manuel Vargas y la Perla los grabaron en la primera mitad del siglo XX, y hasta Mairena dejó dos. Chano Lobato, su mayor cultor, los elevó a cante noble y recrea la venta de los cuadros que popularizó Pericón.

scenes.name: Las tonás: martinetes, carceleras y deblas
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Cantes sin acompañamiento, prueba de su antigüedad, en cuartetas octosílabas de intensa carga dramática y origen gitano indiscutible: son crónicas de la miseria, la cárcel y la persecución. Demófilo ya las daba en 1881 por «cantes viejos casi caídos en desuso»; en el siglo XIX hubo entre veintisiete y treinta y cuatro, cada una con el nombre de su creador. La más antigua es la de Tío Luis el de la Juliana, aguador y primer cantaor del que hay noticia (segunda mitad del siglo XVIII), conservada por Antonio Chacón y recreada por Pepe de la Matrona; se le atribuye también la toná de los pajaritos, que recuerda la tonada sefardí de los bilbilicos. Los martinetes toman el nombre del martillo de la fragua, aunque es difícil cantar mientras se forja: Tío Juane de Jerez montaba una fragua en escena en los setenta y ochenta, y Antonio el Bailarín creó su baile con martillo y yunque; la familia fragüera más antigua es la de los Cantorales de Cádiz, que Silverio visitaba. Las carceleras cantan la prisión y servían para pasar mensajes en romaní desde las rejas. La debla, único palo con nombre romaní («diosa»), es religiosa, casi perdida y muy difícil; llegó a hoy por Tomás Pavón en los cuarenta y la recuperó Antonio Mairena.

scenes.name: Las sevillanas
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Nacen de las seguidillas castellanas, que en Sevilla se hicieron más vivas y fáciles de repetir: cuatro coplas para bailar en pareja un galanteo, con temas andaluces, amorosos o rocieros (corraleras, rocieras, bíblicas, de feria, marineras, romeras). Lorca recogió una del siglo XVIII. Su gran auge comercial llegó en los setenta, con millones de discos que daban envidia a los flamencos; las han grabado con jondura Manuel Vallejo, la Niña de los Peines, la Paquera de Jerez, el Turronero, Chiquetete y Camarón.

scenes.name: El fandango
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Muy apreciado por su musicalidad y fácil de interpretar, no es un palo básico pero no es menor: la vieja división entre cantes grandes y chicos está obsoleta, y la jondura la pone el intérprete, no la antigüedad del palo. Canto para bailar de origen muy antiguo e incierto (Corominas lo deriva del portugués fado; hay quien le ve un lejano origen árabe), aparece por escrito en un entremés de 1705 y lo describe el deán Manuel Martí en 1712; en el siglo XIX fue el cante y baile nacional español, y a finales de siglo se aflamencó en Andalucía y dejó de bailarse. De él salen las granaínas, las malagueñas y los cantes de Levante, y hay fandangos propios en Lucena, Cabra, Puente Genil, Jaén, Granada o Almería. Su apogeo en la ópera flamenca lo desprestigió tanto que a cantaores como Pepe Menese les parece un insulto que se lo pidan; desde los años ochenta se revaloriza.

facts.title: "The Young Ones" Satirical Gag (1982)
facts.body: The widespread cultural phenomenon of "Ashes to Ashes" in the UK led to references in popular media, including a throwaway gag on the satirical British punk comedy show "The Young Ones" a couple of years after its release, highlighting its pervasive recognition. "Ashes to Ashes was a true UK phenomenon, the kind that invited injuks, such as this throwaway gag, a couple of years later, on the satirical British punk comedy show The Young Ones."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.episode: Starman to Blackstar Edition Part 2
facts.name: David Bowie

facts.title: "Cat People" Production Discontent (1982)
facts.body: David Bowie was unhappy with Giorgio Moroder's production of "Cat People (Putting Out Fire)," despite critics calling it one of Bowie's best vocal performances. This discontent led him to ask Nile Rogers to re-record the track with a "crunchier" backing for his subsequent album. "However, David Bowie was unhappy with Moroder's production, and he asked the producer of his next album, Nile Rogers, to re-record Cat People with a new, crunchier backing track."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.episode: Starman to Blackstar Edition Part 2
facts.name: David Bowie

facts.title: Nile Rogers Collaboration Origin (1982)
facts.body: David Bowie met Nile Rogers, the former mastermind of disco band Chic, at a New York club in 1982 and invited him to write and record in Montreux, Switzerland. Bowie sought Rogers to shake up his sound after leaving RCA, explicitly stating he wanted to record the biggest hits of his career. "David Bowie had met Nile Rogers, former mastermind of disco band Sheik, at a New York club in 1982, and he invited Nile to write and record with him in Montreux, Switzerland."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.episode: Starman to Blackstar Edition Part 2
facts.name: David Bowie

facts.title: Peak Popularity and MTV Influence (1982-1983)
facts.body: New Wave experienced its peak popularity in 1982 and 1983, a period significantly bolstered by the debut of MTV in 1981 and MuchMusic in 1983. These music video channels provided a new visual platform for music, turning "telegenic New Wave bands" like Flock of Seagulls, Eurythmics, and Duran Duran into major stars. "New Wave was at its biggest through 1982 and 1983. The music video certainly helped too."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Etymology: Part 1
facts.name: New Wave

facts.title: A "Different Wave" in 1982
facts.body: In 1982, artists like Joe Jackson, Elvis Costello, Graham Parker, and Nick Lowe were charting a "different wave" of New Wave that defied confinement to traditional rock, pop, jazz, or soul categories, distinct from the prevailing synth pop and MTV-driven New Wave of the era. "Joe Jackson, Elvis Costello, Graham Parker and their peer, Nick Lowe were charting a different wave. One that couldn't be confined to rock, pop, jazz or soul."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.episode: Angry Young Men Edition Part 1
facts.name: New Wave

facts.title: Band Formation (1982)
facts.body: The core members, Tom York, Colin Greenwood, and Ed O'Brien, first met and started playing together in their final year at Abingdon, a private school in Oxford, around 1982. At this time, they were approximately 14 or 15 years old. Their initial setup included "three guitarists and a bad drum machine named Dr. Rhythm," and their very first gig was at a friend's birthday party. "Their first gig was at a friends birthday party. This would be sometime in 1982, which means everybody was about 14, 15 years old at the time."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Radiohead - A History: Part 1

facts.title: Joe Strummer's Disappearance (1982)
facts.body: Joe Strummer, a key voice of the British punk explosion, inexplicably vanished on April 26, 1982, the night before The Clash was due to leave on a major tour, forcing the tour to be scrapped. He was gone for eight full weeks, showing up suddenly in mid-May 1982, offering various unconfirmed explanations like running the Paris marathon or helping a girlfriend's mother out of jail, leading to speculation about a publicity stunt or burnout; this vanishing act retrospectively marked the beginning of the end for the band. "Joe Strummer, one of the voices of the whole British punk explosion had inexplicably disappeared, vanished."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 2
facts.name: The Clash

facts.title: Possible Influence from Rashid Taha (1982)
facts.body: After a 1982 show in Paris, Algerian singer-songwriter Rashid Taha, leader of the French Arab-punk band Residence Permit, gave Joe Strummer a demo cassette. A year later, Taha noted stylistic similarities between his demo and "Rock the Casbah," leading to speculation about whether The Clash drew inspiration from his material, though Taha never expressed bitterness and even covered the song himself. "Was Rock the Casbah inspired by what was handed to Joe on that sidewalk that night? Maybe."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Stupid History 2
facts.name: The Clash

facts.title: Topper Headon's Dismissal (May 10, 1982)
facts.body: Drummer Topper Headon was let go on May 10, 1982, due to his "monstrous heroin habit." "First it was Jermore Topper Heaton, who had a monstrous heroin habit. He was let go on May 10th, 1982."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: You're Fired!
facts.name: The Clash

facts.title: Joe Strummer's Disappearance (March-May 1982)
facts.body: In March 1982, Joe Strummer suddenly disappeared for eight weeks after a phone interview with a journalist, leading to a tour cancellation and uncertainty about his well-being. This event occurred just before the release of *Combat Rock*. It was later rumored to be a publicity stunt orchestrated by the band's manager, with Joe reportedly spending his time in France to help a girlfriend bail her mother out of jail.
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Joe Strummer: A Remembrance
facts.name: The Clash

facts.title: Commercially Funky Direction and Expanded Lineup (1982)
facts.body: David Byrne, reportedly envious of Tom Tom Club's success, decided to take Talking Heads in a "commercially funky direction" upon Chris Frantz and Tina Weymouth's return in 1982. They self-produced *Speaking in Tongues* and added "seasoned black players" like guitarist Alex Weir, percussionist Steve Scales, and synth player Bernie Worrell, leading to their most commercially successful music. "When France and Weymouth returned to the talking heads fold in 1982, leader David Bern, reportedly envious of Tom Tom Club's success, decided to take the band in its own commercially funky direction."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.episode: This Ain’t No Party! Edition Part 2
facts.name: The Talking Heads

facts.title: Indie Roots and Mainstream Growth (1982-1985)
facts.body: R.E.M. started as a no-name indie band from the Deep South, releasing their first records on Hib-Tone before moving to IRS Records, an indie label run by Miles Copeland. Between 1982 and 1985, they released five albums on IRS, earning respect as pioneers of the college rock scene in North America, while also gaining a mainstream following due to their accessible music. "R.E.M. released five albums on IRS between 1982 and 1985, and during that time they grew to be one of the most respected alternative bands in North America."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 8

facts.title: Thriller (1982) - Barrier-Breaking Achievement
facts.body: The album *Thriller* is fascinating not just for its incredible quality, but for how Michael Jackson pushed beyond his own perceived limits and achieved something previously unimaginable in the music industry. It marked a significant personal and professional breakthrough for him, setting a new standard. "el thriller de Michael Jackson es apasionante, no tanto por lo increíble que es el disco, por lo bueno que es el disco sino por cómo Michael Jackson consigue romper sus propias barreras y llegar a algo que jamás nadie se imaginó."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: Cómo Michael Jackson hizo el disco más vendido de la historia
facts.name: Michael Jackson

facts.title: Songwriters Hall of Fame Induction (1982)
facts.body: Bob Dylan was inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame in 1982, and notably, the only person he would allow to be photographed with him at the event was Dina Shore. When asked why, Dylan stated it was so his mother would finally acknowledge his success. "in 1982 Bob Dylan was inducted into the song writers Hall of Fame and the only person that he would have his photo. Taken with was Dina sure even she was a little bit shocked about that when he was asked why he said so my mother will finally think I'm somebody."
facts.source: For the Record - The 70s
facts.episode: Ep. 56 - Talk Shows of the 1970s
facts.name: Bob Dylan

facts.title: The Haçienda Nightclub (1982–1997) – Millions Lost, Band Driven to Near-Bankruptcy
facts.body: In 1982, New Order were convinced to invest in building and running a nightclub in their Manchester hometown called the Haçienda. Having no knowledge of club management, they poured millions of pounds into the venture across 15 years, nearly bankrupting themselves. All their New Order and Joy Division album revenues were effectively swallowed by it. The club was culturally important as ground zero for the rave and dance culture explosion of the late 1980s, but was plagued by financial losses, security problems, and drug-related deaths (patrons preferring ecstasy over alcohol made the bar nearly unviable). It closed permanently in June 1997 and was converted to condominiums. Bassist Peter Hook wrote a book about the experience called *How Not to Run a Club*. "The profits of which were largely lost in the sinkhole that was the Haçienda nightclub."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: 10 Terrible Career Moves
facts.name: New Order

facts.title: Financial Support for The Haçienda (1982-1997)
facts.body: New Order's record sales were instrumental in keeping The Haçienda nightclub afloat financially between its opening in 1982 and its closure in 1997, as the club itself was a "money pit." "Between 1982 and 1997, the place was kept afloat by New Order's record sales."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 1
facts.name: New Order

facts.title: Musical Evolution (1982)
facts.body: Initially, New Order sounded similar to Joy Division. However, a trip to New York, where they were exposed to post-disco, early house, and electro music, changed their direction. They became fascinated with synthesizers, drum machines, and sequencers, shifting by 1982 from Joy Division's guitar-based style to a more electronic and dance-oriented sound with Bernard Sumner fronting the band. "And by 1982, New Order had moved away from the guitar-based material that Joy Division had become famous for into something more electronic and dancing, all with Bernard out front."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Groups That Changed Their Front-Person and Survived
facts.name: New Order

facts.title: Founding The Haçienda (1982)
facts.body: Rob Gretton was one of the key figures who conceptualized New Order opening their own nightclub in Manchester. This idea materialized into The Haçienda, which opened in 1982 in a former yacht showroom. While it became a central point of the Manchester music scene and a significant part of the 1980s DJ culture, it was a "complete and utter financial disaster" from its inception, costing New Order millions of pounds.
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Mighty Managers of Rock
facts.name: New Order

facts.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 1
facts.name: New Order

facts.title: Founding The Haçienda (1982)
facts.body: Rob Gretton was one of the key figures who conceptualized New Order opening their own nightclub in Manchester. This idea materialized into The Haçienda, which opened in 1982 in a former yacht showroom. While it became a central point of the Manchester music scene and a significant part of the 1980s DJ culture, it was a "complete and utter financial disaster" from its inception, costing New Order millions of pounds.
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Mighty Managers of Rock
facts.name: New Order

facts.title: Musical Evolution (1982)
facts.body: Initially, New Order sounded similar to Joy Division. However, a trip to New York, where they were exposed to post-disco, early house, and electro music, changed their direction. They became fascinated with synthesizers, drum machines, and sequencers, shifting by 1982 from Joy Division's guitar-based style to a more electronic and dance-oriented sound with Bernard Sumner fronting the band. "And by 1982, New Order had moved away from the guitar-based material that Joy Division had become famous for into something more electronic and dancing, all with Bernard out front."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Groups That Changed Their Front-Person and Survived
facts.name: New Order

facts.title: The Haçienda Nightclub (1982–1997) – Millions Lost, Band Driven to Near-Bankruptcy
facts.body: In 1982, New Order were convinced to invest in building and running a nightclub in their Manchester hometown called the Haçienda. Having no knowledge of club management, they poured millions of pounds into the venture across 15 years, nearly bankrupting themselves. All their New Order and Joy Division album revenues were effectively swallowed by it. The club was culturally important as ground zero for the rave and dance culture explosion of the late 1980s, but was plagued by financial losses, security problems, and drug-related deaths (patrons preferring ecstasy over alcohol made the bar nearly unviable). It closed permanently in June 1997 and was converted to condominiums. Bassist Peter Hook wrote a book about the experience called *How Not to Run a Club*. "The profits of which were largely lost in the sinkhole that was the Haçienda nightclub."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: 10 Terrible Career Moves
facts.name: New Order

facts.title: Early Characteristics (Pre-1982)
facts.body: Before about 1982, industrial music was characterized by the "cold, clanging and banging" sounds pioneered by bands like Throbbing Gristle and Einstürzende Neubauten. "Before about 1982, industrial music was the domain of bands like Throbbing Crystal and I was ending Noe Bowden with their cold, clanging and banging."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 3: Industrial
facts.name: Industrial

facts.title: UK Influence and Guitar-Based Pop Revival (1982-1987)
facts.body: Between 1982 and 1987, The Smiths were one of the most influential UK bands, credited with almost single-handedly rescuing guitar-based pop music from extinction in the UK at a time when synthesizers dominated. They distinguished themselves by crafting guitar-driven songs featuring strong hooks and intense lyrics, becoming icons and heroes to a generation of disaffected and alienated alternative fans. "Between 1982 and 1987, the Smiths almost single-handedly rescued guitar-based pop music from extinction in the UK."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 6
facts.name: The Smiths

facts.title: Live Debut (October 4, 1982)
facts.body: The Smiths made their live debut on October 4, 1982, at The Ritz, a club in Manchester. The lineup eventually settled with Morrissey, Marr, Mike Joyce, and Andy Rourke by the time their first single was released the following spring. "The Smiths made their live debut on October 4th, 1982 at a Manchester club called The Ritz."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: First Compact Disc Player, CDP 101 (October 1, 1982)
facts.body: Sony introduced the world's first compact disc player, the CDP 101, on the afternoon of October 1, 1982. The "CDP" stands for Compact Disk Player, and "101" is binary for the number 5, indicating it was considered a mid-range model in Sony's anticipated future lineup. "Back on the afternoon of October 1st, 1982, Sony introduced a new home stereo gizmo. It was the world's first compact display. They called it the CDP 101."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Rise and Fall of the CD
facts.name: Sony Music

facts.title: Japanese CD Market Launch (October 1, 1982)
facts.body: On October 1, 1982, Sony Japan initiated a significant market launch by issuing 50 compact disc titles simultaneously. "On October 1, 1982, Sony Japan issued 50 titles all at once."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Rise and Fall of the CD

facts.title: First CD Machine - CDP-101 (1982)
facts.body: By late 1982, the compact disk technology was ready, and Sony released the first CD player, the CDP-101. This machine went on sale for about $700. It offered instant track skipping, a revolutionary feature at the time, providing direct access to any song on the disk without fast-forwarding or rewinding. `"By late 1982, the technology was ready. And the first machine, the Sony CDP-101, went on sale for about 700 bucks."`
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The History of Portable Music: Part 1
facts.name: Sony Music

facts.title: Tragic Deaths of Band Members (1982)
facts.body: Within two years of the band's 1980 debut, two of The Pretenders' four members died. Dick Varnedon was fired due to drug abuse and subsequently died from it on June 14, 1982. Just two days later, James Honeyman-Scott died from heart failure, also brought on by drug abuse, a stark example of the "rock and roll lifestyle's" complications. "Dick Varnedon who was fired because of his drug abuse and died from the same on June 14, 1982. Two days later, James Honeyman Scott died from heart failure brought on by drug abuse."
facts.source: For the Record - The 70s
facts.episode: Ep. 43 - Music and The Kent State Massacre of May 4, 1970
facts.name: The Pretenders

facts.title: Controversial Tour with The Clash (September 1982)
facts.body: The Clash embarked on a big stadium and arena tour with The Who in September 1982, a move that surprised and alienated many fans. This was particularly controversial given The Clash's long-standing slogan since 1977, "No Beatles, Elvis, or Rolling Stones," which suggested a rejection of rock establishment figures like The Who. The tour highlighted the growing internal tensions and shifts in The Clash's artistic direction.
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

The ad described an "awesome garage of sound and light" that would "rip through you in a rage of heavy metal fury," encouraging attendees to "Enter the world of a madman." The face value of a ticket for this event was $9 in 1982. "The 1982 Sunom rates Aussie Osborne in the flesh. This Tuesday at the auditorium an awesome garage of sound in light will rip through you in a rage of heavy metal fury."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Weird History of Concert Tickets Part 1
facts.name: Ozzy Osbourne

facts.name: Thriller

facts.title: Most Sold Album of All Time
facts.body: *Thriller*, acknowledged as one of the best and the most sold albums in history, was a product of Michael Jackson's extraordinarily demanding and professional work ethic, not solely his immense talent. The recording process for *Thriller* involved assembling an elite team, including over 50 of the best musicians, important rock artists, and direct collaborations with figures like Eddie Van Halen and Paul McCartney, all under the guidance of Quincy Jones. "Michael Jackson grabó el thriller gracias a un trabajo durísimo y terriblemente profesional que le permitió llegar a esos niveles de calidad."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: Cómo Michael Jackson hizo el disco más vendido de la historia
facts.name: Thriller

facts.title: Extensive Production and Collaboration
facts.body: For the *Thriller* album, Michael Jackson assembled an elite team, including over 50 of the best musicians available at the moment, important rock artists, and directly called upon Eddie Van Halen and Paul McCartney. He also relied on Quincy Jones, described as the best producer of Black music in history. Despite recording up to 30 songs, Jackson was so demanding that he felt none were good enough, ultimately selecting only nine tracks for the final album. "Michael Jackson para hacer el thriller cogió a más de 50 músicos que eran casi los mejores músicos que había en el momento. Me refiero cogió músicos ellas, importantes, cogió artistas de rock, importantes, incluso llamó al mismísimo Eddie Van Halen, llamó Paul McCartney, me refiero ser rodeo de lo mejor que pudo encontrar."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: Cómo Michael Jackson hizo el disco más vendido de la historia
facts.name: Thriller

facts.title: Post-Recording Dissatisfaction and Remixing
facts.body: Despite the immense effort and resources invested in recording *Thriller*, Michael Jackson was initially dissatisfied with the results, feeling the songs were not "good enough" or even "bad." He and Quincy Jones spent an entire extra week remixing every song on the album from scratch. Even after this extensive rework, Jackson remained unconvinced of the album's perfection, ultimately releasing it without his full satisfaction. "Michael Jackson terminó sacando el disco sin estar convencido de que fue ese suficientemente bueno para lo que quería hacer."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: Cómo Michael Jackson hizo el disco más vendido de la historia
facts.name: Thriller

facts.title: Genesis of Modern Pop
facts.body: The release of *Thriller* marked a pivotal moment, officially commencing the era of mainstream pop music and mass-market pop stars, preceding the emergence of other major pop figures like Madonna. Michael Jackson reinvented numerous aspects that would define pop music moving forward, from dance choreography to music videos and large-scale concert performances. "el pop de gran consumo o la época gradada de la música pop empieza oficialmente con el thriller, poco después empezaría a venir las grandes super estrellas del pop vendría madona, vendría a todas las grandes estrellas del pop, Michael Jackson abrió una nueva manera de hacer el pop de gran consumo."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan

facts.body: This album achieved monumental success, spending "37 weeks at number one" on the charts and eventually outselling both Fleetwood Mac's "Rumours" and The Bee Gees' "Saturday Night Fever" soundtrack. facts.title: Post-Disco Backlash Comeback (1982-1984)
facts.body: In the wake of the 1979 disco backlash, dance music (which pop fans carefully avoided calling "disco") began making a strong comeback on the charts by late 1983 and early 1984, doing better than it had since 1979. This resurgence was driven by new wave synth pop, Michael Jackson's success, and sleek club styles from artists like The Pointer Sisters, Shannon, and Madonna. "By late 83 and early 84 dance music, which is what we called it then, pop fans were careful never to say the other five letter D word. And it was doing better on the charts than it had since 1979."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.episode: What’s 1984 Got to Do with It Edition Part 1
facts.name: dance

facts.title: Formation and Unique Sound (1982)
facts.body: Formed in Vancouver in 1982, Skinny Puppy quickly developed a distinctive sound incorporating keyboards, samplers that used clips from horror movies, drum machines, and loud guitars. The band is considered crucial to the development of the modern industrial sound, perhaps more so than any other early 80s group. "They were formed at Vancouver in 1982 and almost immediately carved out their own special sound with keyboards and samplers that took clips from horror movies. They had drum machines and they had loud guitars."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 3: Industrial
facts.name: Skinny Puppy

facts.title: Impact on UK Musicians Union (1982)
facts.body: Barry Manilow's decision to replace his orchestra with synthesizers during his tours sparked outrage within the UK Musicians Union in 1982. This move was a primary catalyst for the union to pass a motion demanding that synthesizers be banned, viewing them as a threat to musicians' livelihoods. "The problem was this guy. In 1982, Barry Manolo was a huge star."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Music vs Technology Over The Years
facts.name: Barry Manilow

facts.title: Jazz Coleman Quits for Apocalypse (1982)
facts.body: In February 1982, following a performance, singer Jazz Coleman announced his departure from Killing Joke and his intention to move to Iceland. He was convinced that the apocalypse was near and believed Iceland offered the safest refuge. This conviction stemmed from his deep fascination with the occult and a growing paranoia developed after investigating various conspiracy theories concerning the end of the world. Shortly after, guitarist Jordy Walker joined him in Iceland, seemingly persuaded by Coleman's apocalyptic reasoning. "After a gig, he announced he was quitting killing joke and moving to Iceland."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Musicians Who Lost It: Part 2
facts.name: Killing Joke

facts.title: Jaz Coleman's Apocalyptic Beliefs (1982)
facts.body: After the release of the album "Revelations" in 1982, singer Jaz Coleman became convinced that the world was truly about to end. He determined this through various occult means, coincidentally sharing a birthday with cult master Alistair Crowley. "After the album hit the stores, singer jazz Coleman decided that the world really was about to end."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Alt Rocks Craziest People
facts.name: Killing Joke

facts.title: Disappearance to Iceland (1982)
facts.body: Following a gig in Brighton, England, Jaz Coleman suddenly disappeared. He made two phone calls, one to his mother to assure her he was alright and another to Killing Joke's record label. He then traveled to Iceland, believing it to be the safest place on the planet based on his interpretations. "So after a gig in Brighton England he suddenly disappeared."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Alt Rocks Craziest People
facts.name: Killing Joke

facts.title: Severing Ties and Geordie's Support (April 7, 1982)
facts.body: On April 7, 1982, Jaz Coleman released a statement formally severing all his remaining ties with Killing Joke. However, Geordie, the band's guitarist, believed Coleman's apocalyptic theories and flew to Iceland to join him. "On April 7th 1982, Jazz released a statement severing all his remaining ties with Killing Joke."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Alt Rocks Craziest People
facts.name: Killing Joke

facts.title: Seven Months Awaiting Apocalypse (1982)
facts.body: Jaz Coleman and Geordie spent seven months in Iceland, waiting for the apocalypse that never materialized. During this time, they worked with various Icelandic bands, one of which eventually evolved into The Sugarcubes, featuring Björk. After seven months, they gave up and returned to England. "For seven months of wedding for the apocalypse they gave up and went back to England."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Alt Rocks Craziest People
facts.name: Killing Joke

facts.title: `Cafe Flesh` Sample (1982)
facts.body: The distinct moaning in Rob Zombie and White Zombie's song "More Human Than Human" is sampled from the 1982 sci-fi movie `Cafe Flesh`, which depicts a post-nuclear world where most surviving humans become ill if they attempt sex, leading to live sex shows for their benefit. "The sample is taken from a 1982 sci-fi movie called Cafe Flesh. After the world is nearly annihilated in a nuclear war, they're surviving humans find that they get sick when they try to have sex. The moaning comes from someone participating in a live sex show conducted for the benefit of those humans who can't have sex anymore."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Weird and Shocking Rockers
facts.name: Rob Zombie

facts.title: Falklands War Hoax Tape (1982)
facts.body: Crass devised a prank in 1982 by editing speeches from Ronald Reagan and Margaret Thatcher to create a fake phone call that made it sound as if they were plotting a wider war against the Soviet Union, with Thatcher also appearing to take responsibility for the sinking of an Argentine battleship during the Falklands War. This idea stemmed from classified information shared by a former skinhead sailor who had served in the Falklands. Crass secretly sent the tape to newspapers across Europe. "Based on what they heard from this sailor, Crasse, who wrote it down, they took notes, came up with the idea of cutting together some speeches by Ronald Reagan and Margaret Fatcher to make it sound like a phone call between the two of them, sometime, allegedly, in 1982."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Great KGB Punk Rock Conspiracy
facts.name: Crass

facts.title: Invitation to Russian Literary Magazine (1982)
facts.body: Shortly after their Falklands War hoax was uncovered in 1982, Crass was invited to a meeting at a supposed Russian literary magazine in London. This event, combined with subsequent approaches from various intelligence and radical groups, fueled suspicion within British intelligence about potential Soviet contact. "Crasse was invited to a meeting at a supposed Russian literary magazine in London."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Great KGB Punk Rock Conspiracy
facts.name: Crass

facts.body: For *Beat It*, Michael Jackson deliberately expanded his musical style, incorporating rock elements and synthesizer music, genres he hadn't extensively worked with before. After auditioning numerous guitarists for the electric guitar part, he called Eddie Van Halen. Jackson made Van Halen try 30 different guitars to achieve the exact sound he envisioned for the song's chords, a process Van Halen described as an unparalleled "fetishism of sound." "Michael Jackson acabó llamando al mismo de Divaan Hallen al cual lo hizo probar 30 guitarras distintas hasta que encontró a Eddie Van Hallen y encontró la guitarra que Michael Jackson quería para cómo sonaba en el beat."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan

facts.name: Beat It

facts.body: The video for "Beat It" was crucial in breaking MTV's unofficial color barrier. After CBS Records allegedly threatened to withdraw all their videos from the channel, MTV caved and began showing clips from the "Thriller" album, including "Beat It." Its appearance led to "Thriller" selling 200,000 copies a week. "Once the clip for Beaded appeared, thriller started selling 200,000 copies a week."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
